title: Phishing & Social Engineering Security Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect against phishing scams and social engineering attacks. Learn to recognize threats and secure your accounts.
intro: Phishing and social engineering attacks target human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. This checklist helps you recognize common tactics and implement protective measures to safeguard your personal information and accounts.

items.task: Always verify sender identity before clicking links or attachments
items.why: Attackers often impersonate trusted organizations to steal credentials or install malware on your device.
items.howTo: Check the sender's email address carefully for misspellings or suspicious domains. When in doubt, contact the organization directly through their official website or phone number.

items.task: Hover over links to preview destinations before clicking
items.why: Malicious links often redirect to fake websites designed to steal your login credentials or personal information.
items.howTo: Place your mouse over any link without clicking to see the actual URL. Look for suspicious domains, misspellings, or URLs that don't match the claimed destination.

items.why: Email attachments are a common way to distribute malware that can compromise your device and steal sensitive data.
items.howTo: Only open attachments from trusted senders that you were expecting. Scan all attachments with antivirus software before opening, even from known contacts.

items.task: Be skeptical of urgent or threatening language in emails
items.why: Scammers use urgency and fear tactics to pressure you into making quick decisions without proper verification.
items.howTo: Take time to verify any urgent requests through official channels. Legitimate organizations rarely demand immediate action via email for security issues.

items.task: Enable two-factor authentication on all important accounts
items.why: Even if attackers steal your password through phishing, 2FA provides an additional security layer that's much harder to bypass.
items.howTo: Go to security settings for each account and enable 2FA using an authenticator app like Google Authenticator or Authy. Avoid SMS-based 2FA when possible.

items.task: Use unique, strong passwords for every account
items.why: If one account is compromised through phishing, unique passwords prevent attackers from accessing your other accounts.
items.howTo: Use a reputable password manager to generate and store unique passwords for each account. Make passwords at least 12 characters with mixed characters.

items.task: Monitor accounts regularly for suspicious activity
items.why: Early detection of unauthorized access allows you to quickly secure compromised accounts before significant damage occurs.
items.howTo: Check bank statements, credit reports, and account activity regularly. Set up account alerts for login attempts and transactions when available.

items.task: Use privacy-focused browsers for sensitive activities
items.why: Privacy browsers provide better protection against tracking and malicious websites that may be used in social engineering attacks.
items.howTo: Consider using Incognito Browser for banking and sensitive activities. It blocks trackers and provides enhanced privacy protection compared to standard browsers.

items.task: Verify identity before sharing sensitive information
items.why: Social engineers often impersonate authority figures or trusted contacts to manipulate you into revealing confidential information.
items.howTo: Always verify requests through a separate communication channel. Call the person or organization directly using a number you trust, not one provided in the request.

items.task: Limit personal information shared on social media
items.why: Attackers use publicly available personal information to make their social engineering attempts more convincing and targeted.
items.howTo: Review privacy settings on all social media accounts. Avoid posting personal details like full birth dates, addresses, or information about security questions.

items.task: Question unexpected requests from authority figures
items.why: Social engineers often pose as IT support, managers, or government officials to exploit your natural tendency to comply with authority.
items.howTo: Politely ask for verification when contacted by someone claiming authority. Request their name, department, and callback number to verify through official channels.

items.task: Trust your instincts when something feels suspicious
items.why: Your intuition often detects subtle inconsistencies that your conscious mind might miss in social engineering attempts.
items.howTo: If something feels off about a request or interaction, pause and investigate further. It's better to be cautious than to become a victim of fraud.

items.task: Keep emergency contact information readily available
items.why: Quick response to security incidents can minimize damage and help you recover faster from successful attacks.
items.howTo: Maintain a list of important phone numbers for banks, credit card companies, and other critical services. Store this information securely offline.

items.task: Create an action plan for suspected phishing incidents
items.why: Having a predetermined response plan helps you act quickly and effectively if you suspect you've been targeted or compromised.
items.howTo: Document steps to take if you click a suspicious link or share information: change passwords, contact institutions, monitor accounts, and report incidents.

items.task: Maintain secure backups of important data
items.why: If malware from a phishing attack encrypts your files, secure backups ensure you can recover your important information.
items.howTo: Regularly backup important files to a secure, offline location or encrypted cloud service. Test your backup restoration process periodically.
